title: How to Train Your Elites
author: R. R. Reno
summary: R. R. Reno takes up Aaron Renn's diagnosis that society is troubled by a lousy elite, one selected for technical-professional and managerial-bureaucratic skills, and asks what the Victorian elite did differently. Drawing on Samuel Hughes's essay, he notes that Victorian elites were produced by schools such as Eton and Winchester that were not very academic, had little STEM, and taught Latin and Greek, while Oxbridge "pass men" followed undemanding tracks and an Oxford tutor could say a PhD "ruined a man". Reno recalls his Yale mentor George Lindbeck lamenting the demise of the gentleman C student. He argues that the aim of elite formation was social virtue, self-assertion balanced by loyalty and competitiveness guided by responsibility. He acknowledges the snobbery and insularity of the old system but says it produced the leaders of twentieth-century America and echoes Plato's guardians, and he concludes that the lesson is about formation of character more than credentials.
points: Victorian elites were formed by character-focused, classical, non-STEM schooling rather than by being math champions or valedictorians.
The "gentleman C student" reflects an older ideal in which breadth, sociability and amateurism mattered more than academic professionalism.
The main product of that formation was social virtue: self-assertion with loyalty, competitiveness with responsibility.
Reno concedes the system's snobbery and insularity but credits it with the leaders who built twentieth-century American pre-eminence.
Selecting for technical skill alone, he suggests, yields leaders strong at optimising and weak at governing.
quotes: Shrill online extremism. Protesters who can’t name the river or the sea in their chants. University students demanding safe spaces.

Renn cites Vivek Ramaswamy’s notorious 2024 tweet, which criticized America’s priorities. The entrepreneur-turned-political-candidate wrote: “A culture that celebrates the prom queen over the math olympiad champ, or the jock over the valedictorian, will not produce the best engineers.

More impressive still, the same Victorian elites and their Edwardian successors steered Britain through the social tumult of the Industrial Revolution “with none of the revolutions and civil wars that wracked continental Europe.
One of my PhD mentors, George Lindbeck, began teaching at Yale in the early 1950s. I recall asking him what the biggest change had been during his long career.

Hughes notes that most nineteenth-century Oxbridge undergraduates were “pass men,” following a track of study that was famously undemanding, allowing them more time for rowing, parties, and competing for social status. This pattern of life continued.

Lawrence Lowell established (and personally endowed) the Society of Fellows at Harvard for the express purpose of protecting the brightest graduate students from what he regarded as the flattening effects of doctoral study—“the mass production of mediocrity,” as he put it.

He was not an impressive student. Perhaps that was to his advantage. Biographers note that as an undergraduate FDR applied his intelligence and ambition to attaining membership in Harvard’s most exclusive student organization, the Porcellian Club.
